newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU summit prospects better after EMU pact progress.
newsitem.headline: EU summit prospects better after EMU pact progress.

text.p: European Union leaders appeared set to paper over a rift in their ranks over economic and monetary union (EMU) on Sunday after their finance ministers reported progress on the eve of a contentious EU summit.

Ministers emerged from a late night dinner on Sunday saying they believed an agreement could be reached on the first day of the bloc's mid-year summit that would meet France's concerns over employment without unravelling EMU's carefully laid plans.
"It was a very fruitful and constructive discussion. I am very optimistic we shall have an agreement," European Commission President Jacques Santer told Reuters.
But others noted the rift between France and Germany over the pact had laid bare the essential differences in the two European powers ahead of monetary union.

"In Germany there is a real distrust of everything political," Luxembourg Premier Jean-Claude Juncker said in an interview to be published in Le Figaro on Monday. "In France there is a real distrust of everything economic."

The ministers were forced into negotiations when France's Socialist government refused to sign up to the Stability Pact, an accord reached in principle in December to stop countries running large deficits after the single currency is launched.
Paris argued that too much attention was being paid to budgetary rigour and not enough to fighting unemployment.

The move irritated France's partners, drove a wedge into the the Franco-German alliance, upset financial markets, and overshadowed the summit which is supposed to agree a new EU treaty to prepare the bloc for enlargement into eastern Europe.
Paris's EU partners have since tried to meet its concerns with a resolution to be attached to the pact.

Few details were available of Sunday night's discussion, but it appeared that France had fallen short at least for now of getting support for large funding projects to chip away at the bloc's double-digit unemployment.
"It's not realistic to think that we could get that," said one prime minister who asked not to be named.
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said the ministers had discussed the possibility of giving the European Investment Bank (EIB), the bloc's main lending arm, a more active role in job creation.
He said it was possible that the EIB would form part of a resolution on employment which was being negotiated by the finance ministers following the French demands for more emphasis on job creation.
Officials said the ministers would meet again late on Monday morning in hope of finishing an agreement to be presented to the EU leaders later in the day.

One issue likely to be discuss was a plan to hold a special jobs summit in Luxembourg in October. The summit would discuss some of the issues left over from the Amsterdam summit as well as underlining France's desire to put employment at the top of the agenda.
Diplomats said the EU leaders would try hard on Monday not to let the rift over monetary union disrupt their negotiations of a new EU treaty.
"They are trying to do it in parallel, but (the row) also affects the mood," one diplomat said.
The treaty is designed to create an area of freedom for the bloc's citizens, prepare EU institutions for enlargement and formally make job creation an EU goal.
